short: A comprehensive survey of English landholdings that cemented Norman administrative control.
full:
Commissioned by William the Conqueror at Christmas 1085, the Domesday Book was a systematic audit of landholdings and resources across England. Royal commissioners travelled throughout the shires, recording who owned each estate before and after the Conquest, its taxable value, and the resources it contained, from plough-teams to woodland. The survey was unparalleled in medieval Europe for its ambition and detail.

The completed manuscript of 1086 provided William with precise knowledge of his kingdom's wealth and a definitive legal record of the massive transfer of land from Anglo-Saxon to Norman hands. It fundamentally reformed royal taxation and bound the new aristocracy directly to the crown. The text remained legally binding for centuries, establishing an administrative foundation that defined English government.
